newsitem.title: CHINA: Bk of East Asia interim seen reasonable, not great.
newsitem.headline: Bk of East Asia interim seen reasonable, not great.

text.p: Blue chip Bank of East Asia is forecast to report good earnings growth for the first six months of the year, although at the lower end of the range for Hong Kong's big banks.

Analysts said the bank's longstanding premium to the rest of the blue chip finance sector is under pressure and most said they will maintain their sell recommendations unless they see "magnificent" earnings.
"Effectively, I am looking for it to be a reasonable year, but (it is) difficult to match last year's," said regional banking analyst Peter Redhead at ING Barings.

Redhead forecast Bank of East Asia would post net profit of HK$927.4 million for the six months to June 30, 1997, up 9.5 percent over the same period last year, when it reports interim earnings on Friday.
The bank's profit rose 23.3 percent in first half 1996.
Other blue chip banks are expected to report earnings growth of between 10 percent and 14 percent for first-half 1997.
Analysts said the chief reason for the slower growth is that Bank of East Asia had to slow growth of its loan portfolio in mortgages and other property-related lending this year.
Otherwise, the bank would exceed regulators' recommended 40 percent weighting for property loans, they said.
Analyst Alan Hutcheson at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said Bank of East Asia has been less aggressive compared to other banks in property lending, still the industry's largest growth sector.
"The Bank of East Asia has enjoyed good growth in property-related lending, but has only been a player rather than a leader in the mortgage war," said Hutcheson.

Over the 26 months or more, local banks slashed their mortgage rates to gain marketshare. In January 1996, the average mortgage rate was prime plus 175 basis points, then fell to prime plus 60 in January 1997, said Hutcheson.
The rate was currently around prime plus 25 points, he said.
At the same time, the Bank of East Asia's loan-to-deposit ratio rose to about 78 percent from 70 percent in 1996, said Hutcheson.
"The bulk of loan growth will come from lower margin but higher risk commercial lending," he said.
"First-half growth should be reasonably good," said Hutcheson added, noting he expected to see slightly slower growth in the second half of the year.
Hutcheson expects the bank to report full year earnings of HK$2.03 billion, an 8.14 percent rise over 1996. He did not have a half year forecast.
Many analysts see the bank as overvalued at these levels and requiring fairly "magnificent" earnings growth to change their recommendations to buy from the current sell ratings.
The bank has been able to maintain its premium rating due to its status as having the best China plan in the Hong Kong financial sector, said ING's Redhead.
But other local banks have expanded their exposure to China and the bank has lost its pioneer advantage, analysts said.

Having initially focused on growth in residential mortgages to Hong Kong people for property in China, the bank has branched out to trade finance, project finance and hire purchase businesses in China, said Hutchison.
"Mainland mortgage demand is slowing, while margins are under pressure," said Hutcheson. "At the same time, BEA's new growth avenues, such as trade finance, are subject to increasing competition."
China operations contributed roughly 12 percent of the bank's earnings in 1996.
Bank of East Asia closed unchanged at HK$32.50 on Wednesday.
